title: Tourette's film I Swear wins three Scottish Baftas
content:
I Swear was the big winner at the Bafta Scotland awards on Sunday.
The film about Tourette syndrome campaigner John Davidson won Best Film, Best Director and Best Actor.
The condition causes involuntary vocal and physical tics and, in Davidson's case, coprolalia, which causes him to shout offensive and inappropriate phrases.
Davidson was at the centre of controversy when he attended the Bafta film awards earlier this year. His shouts, which included a racial slur, were heard in the hall during the event and broadcast in the BBC coverage of the event.
Davidson, from Galashiels, said he had been deeply affected by the experience but was determined to attend the awards in Glasgow, where I Swear was nominated in six categories.
" I didn't want to give people the impression I was hiding away," he said.
"So I spoke to Bafta Scotland and said 'how can we can make it easy, less stressful, and less complicated than it was in London?'".
The answer was to brief guests about Davidson's condition.
A Bafta Scotland staff member was with him during any interactions with members of the public.
Davidson, his family and friends, watched the awards via video link from a separate room in the Glasgow hotel where the ceremony took place.
Davidson said he hoped the film would raise awareness and increase understanding of the condition, which affects about 300,000 people in the UK.
I Swear's director, Kirk Jones, thanked the town of Galashiels and Tourette's groups in Scotland for supporting the film as he picked up the first of three awards.
He also paid tribute to John Davidson for sharing his story.
"I know it's been a long and difficult journey," he said. "Thank you for having the strength to continue that journey and for stressing the importance of acceptance and empathy at a time when the world desperately needs it."
He added: "My big hope was that it would help people understand those with Tourette's.
"What I didn't realise was that there's a much wider community of people with neurodiverse conditions who have connected with the film and feel for the first time there's a representation of a condition which is often hidden."
For Davidson, Sunday's wins are the celebration he was hoping for at the Baftas earlier this year.
"Tonight's not really about me, although it is my story," he said.
"It's about celebrating the actors and a beautiful film. I was blown away when I first saw it. I've never watched it since because it makes me cry.
"So I'm chuffed to bits that it's won tonight."

title: Robert Pattinson chosen as the next James Bond
content: The name’s Pattinson, Robert Pattinson . After months of intense rumors of a casting battle between some of the entertainment industry’s top names , actor Robert Pattinson, known for his roles in this year’s “The Odyssey” and “The Drama” — not to mention “Twilight” of years gone by — was announced as the next James Bond by Amazon MGM Studios via the official 007 website Monday. “James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime,” the 40-year-old British actor said in a statement. “To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement.” The news of Pattinson’s casting was accompanied by a teaser clip of him as Bond — dressed, naturally, in a tuxedo and pointing a gun — as the series’ iconic theme song played. Pattinson joins an elite club: Just six actors have portrayed 007. Sean Connery first appeared as the suave secret agent in 1962’s “Dr. No.” The most recent was Daniel Craig, who appeared as Bond in five films over 15 years, starting with 2006’s “Casino Royale” and most recently in 2021’s “No Time to Die.” Production on the next Bond movie, the still-untitled 26th in the series, will begin soon under the direction of French-Canadian director Denis Villeneuve, who is also behind the “Dune” trilogy — the third installment of which costars Pattinson and comes out next month. “We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007,” Villeneuve said in the statement, adding that Pattinson “has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new.” To say that Pattinson has had a stellar year is an understatement. In addition to “The Drama” and “The Odyssey,” the actor is also courting awards buzz for his chilling portrayal of “To Catch a Predator” creator Chris Hansen in this fall’s “ Primetime .” He’s also been filming as another legendary character, namely Bruce Wayne/Batman, in the upcoming “The Batman: Part II.” (“The Batman: Part II” comes from Warner Bros., which is owned by CNN’s parent company.) Craig’s last turn as Bond in 2021’s “No Time to Die” ended with a closing credit promise that “James Bond will return.” Speculation over the next Bond simmered ever since. Yet for five years, Bond has been MIA while his corporate handlers went to battle. In 2022, Amazon paid more than $8.56 billion for Bond’s parent company, MGM, and thus the rights to distribute the 007 movies, but tensions soon emerged. Barbara Broccoli — who maintained creative control of the character thanks to a deal her late father, Albert “Cubby” Broccoli, had made with novelist Ian Fleming, the inventor of Bond — was reportedly highly distrustful of the data-driven Amazon, resulting in a standoff, according to a 2024 report in the Wall Street Journal . The impasse was broken a year later when a new deal was announced to finally hand creative control of the character to Amazon MGM Studios for an undisclosed sum, ending the Broccoli family’s control over 007 after more than 60 years. After that, the hunt for the next Bond began gathering steam. Casting officially began in May of this year, while second-round auditions were said to have been held in August . Some of the biggest young stars in film were soon rumored to be in contention — although none were officially confirmed as potentials. Names floated in the press included Harris Dickinson, Callum Turner, Paul Mescal, Tom Holland, Jack Lowden, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Henry Cavill, Theo James and Jacob Elordi. One major question long hung over the next Bond: was it time for 007 to be played by a man of color? For years, fans of Idris Elba had championed him to play the next iteration of Bond, although as time went on the now-54-year-old actor seemed to age out of the role, especially given it would likely require stunt-heavy sequels. Still, the names of other younger actors were floated , including Dev Patel, Henry Golding, Regé-John Page and Daniel Kaluuya. As casting continued, Elba seemed to shut down the idea of a non-white Bond as unrealistic and said the rumors around him were never based in truth. “James Bond was written how he was written for a reason,” Elba told GQ in June. “In realistic terms, some markets just don’t go for that,” Elba said of a Black man playing 007. “Bond is big all over the world,” he said. “That’s not what they like in their culture. Period.” No plot details or other casting for the next movie, based on a script from “Peaky Blinders” creator Steven Knight, have been announced. It’s also not yet known if any actors from the previous films may return for what is widely expected to be a reboot of the series.

final_quality.reason: A major entertainment development, the selection of a new James Bond actor is a significant news event that affects a large audience and will spark discussion and analysis.

title: Beatles show keeps music promoter's legacy alive
content:
A new touring show about the Beatles' early years will be a lasting legacy of its writer, the late Stoke-on-Trent music promoter and record shop owner, Mike Lloyd.
The Rise of the Beatles is described as "a gig with narration" and tells the story of the Liverpool band's formation up until the moment they appeared at the King's Hall in Stoke in January 1963.
The gigs were Lloyd's final passion project, before his death in December, and came about after he was asked to do something for the city's centenary celebrations in 2025.
It was intended to be a one-off but is now being revived as a touring production.
Hundreds packed into King's Hall to see it as part of the centenary celebrations, and the new iteration opens at the Mitchell Arts Centre in Hanley on 23 November.
"We've decided that we want to carry on that legacy, because it's such a huge piece of the community that we don't want to let it go," said Lloyd's son Alex, speaking in January about the decision to stage the performances.
Opening at the Mitchell Arts Centre is particularly poignant, as Lloyd was a board member there.
Dave Shingler, friend and former employee, was asked by his family to put the Beatles show on and described it as partly storytelling and partly a tribute to the band.
"He really wanted to do a Beatles show that wasn't like any normal Beatles tribute act," Shingler said.
"He wanted to do something a little bit different – the idea of telling a story as well as putting the music on was at the forefront of it."
He added that he was not sure at first whether they would be able to do it due to all the various aspects of Lloyd's former business they were getting to grips with after his death.
He said he was "constantly second-guessing" whether Lloyd would have made the same decisions he was making but that he had been well supported by Lloyd's family and former colleagues.
"In the back of your head, you've always got, 'What would Mike have done? What would Mike think about this?'
"Every now and then it does hit you that he's not there; he's not coming through the door."
He said the Mitchell Arts Centre was "the best place to start the show" due to Lloyd being on the board there and his love for the venue.
The show continues to Bridgnorth and Telford after Hanley, with plans for other venues after that.

final_quality.reason: The article reports a significant and unique development in the entertainment category, as it highlights a new touring show that celebrates the legacy of a late music promoter and record shop owner. The show's story and music are distinct from typical Beatles tribute acts, making it an interesting and relevant topic for fans of the band and the music industry.
